questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Behaviour and the Processes Inferred From It
questions.learningObjective: state what the discipline takes as its subject matter
questions.stem: A researcher times a person's reaction to a warning sign and also argues about the attention that produced the delay. What does the subject matter of the discipline cover in that project?

options.text: Behaviour and the mental processes inferred from it, since the process is inferred from what can be recorded rather than assumed directly
Only directly observable behaviour, because a private process cannot enter a study at all
options.misconception: narrows the subject to what is visible and treats private events as inadmissible

options.text: The brain structures that produce the delay, since only anatomy counts as a psychology datum
options.misconception: reduces the whole subject to anatomy and drops behaviour from the account

options.text: Only unusual cases, since typical responses reveal nothing about the machinery behind them
options.misconception: assumes only unusual cases carry information and typical responses prove nothing

questions.explanation: The two halves of the project are the same project. The reaction time is a behavioural datum because somebody can record it with a clock, and the attention is a mental process that nobody watches directly, so it is inferred from the pattern of times and the conditions under which they change. The discipline's subject matter is behaviour and the processes inferred from it, and the inference is what makes the subject a science of mind rather than a catalogue of behaviours. The observable-only reading belongs to behaviourism, which was a deliberate and productive restriction for a period rather than a definition of the field, and it does not describe current practice. The anatomy-only reading inverts the relation: the brain is one source of evidence about a process, not a replacement for the behaviour the process is inferred from. The unusual-cases reading is wrong on the evidence: the reason for studying typical performance is that typical performance is the thing an explanation has to cover.
questions.hint: Ask what the second half of the project is doing when it claims to know about attention.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Four Aims Carried Out in One Study
questions.learningObjective: order the aims of describing, explaining, predicting and influencing in a single project
questions.stem: A team studies why shoppers hesitate in front of a display of an unfamiliar fruit. Put the four aims of the discipline in the order the team would carry them out.

options.text: Explain it, proposing that a poor estimate of the fruit's value makes the shopper hesitate
Predict it, checking whether the proposed account forecasts the hesitation in an untested display
Influence it, testing whether a label carrying a price shortens the hesitation
Describe the hesitation, recording when it starts and how long it lasts in front of the display

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by what each aim needs in order to be attempted at all. A description requires nothing but instruments and a decision about what to record, so it comes first and every later aim depends on it. An explanation requires a description to explain, and it is the step that adds a mechanism rather than a record. A prediction is possible only once a mechanism has been stated, because a mechanism is what generates expectations for a case the mechanism has not yet faced; a description alone generates no forecasts. Influence comes last because it is the only aim that has to be tried deliberately and ethically, and because a practice that changes behaviour is worthless if it changes nothing anyone cares about. Putting prediction before explanation fails because there is nothing yet to predict from, and putting influence before description would mean acting on an account nobody has characterised.
questions.hint: Ask which aim has to be satisfied before the next one is even possible.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Two Supported Claims and Two Overstatements
questions.learningObjective: judge which claims about the standing of the discipline are supported
questions.stem: Four claims about the standing of the discipline are offered. Which two are supported? Select both.

options.text: It is a science in the ordinary sense because its claims rest on observations that can be recorded, repeated and contradicted
Values enter the work when a question is chosen, and they do not enter the arithmetic of a measurement once it is made
It cannot be a science at all, since everything studied happens inside a single species that can read the questions
options.misconception: rules out the possibility of science on the ground that the subjects are people

options.text: Measurement is wholly free of the researcher's choices, so a number is never affected by how it was defined
options.misconception: makes a number independent of the operational decision that produced it

questions.explanation: The first claim is what makes the discipline accountable to the ordinary scientific test, which is not that its conclusions are true in advance but that they are attached to evidence a reader can check, repeat and use to break them. A discipline restricted to human subjects has exactly as many opportunities for observation and repetition as any other, and the fact that a participant can read the instructions is a design feature, handled by comparison groups and by not telling the whole story. The second claim separates the two places where judgement enters. Choosing a question is a value judgement about what matters, and nobody pretends otherwise. Once a measure has been chosen, though, the arithmetic applied to the resulting numbers is not a matter of preference, and the requirement that a measurement be repeated exactly is what removes the researcher from the calculation. The human-only argument and the choice-free-measurement argument each overreach in opposite directions, and the truth lies between them.
questions.hint: Ask what the ordinary test for a science is, and then where judgement actually enters the work.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Matching a Question to Its Subfield
questions.learningObjective: sort sample research questions into the subfields that would take them
questions.stem: Four questions are queued for a research group. Which two of them belong to developmental psychology rather than to another subfield?

options.text: Whether the vocabulary a child uses at eighteen months predicts the words she has three years later
Whether adding a second tone to a first changes the pitch a listener reports
options.misconception: describes a change from one stimulus to another and confuses it with change across the lifespan

options.text: Whether two people who describe themselves alike in a personality inventory behave differently at work
options.misconception: takes a present-day trait comparison and treats the trait as something that developed

options.text: What changes in the electrical record between a period of deep sleep and the period after it
options.misconception: reads a difference between two states as evidence about development

questions.explanation: Developmental work is identified by the source of its variation, not by the age of the people in the room. A question counts as developmental when the independent variable is age, a stage, or a time of exposure measured in a person's history, and when the design is arranged so that those things cannot be confounded with the people who happen to have them. The vocabulary question has that shape: the later outcome is the same child's later outcome, and the earlier one is fixed rather than chosen, which is what a developmental prediction looks like. The personality question also has it, because a personality inventory is treated as an outcome with a history behind it. The tone question varies a stimulus, not a person or a period of a life, and belongs with perception. The sleep question varies a state, which is a difference between two conditions of one system, and a difference of that kind is not a difference between two ages.
questions.hint: Ask which items vary something about the person or their history rather than varying the stimulus or the state.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Basic and Applied Research
questions.learningObjective: distinguish research aimed at a decision from research aimed at a description
questions.stem: A company funds a trial of a new training schedule, while a separate laboratory tracks how the number of practices changes a simple motor skill with no practical end in view. Which pairing is right?

options.text: Both are basic work, since applied research is possible only inside a medical rather than an industrial setting
options.misconception: makes the setting of applied work a medical one and excludes industrial settings

options.text: The funded trial is applied work because its target is a decision, and the laboratory study is basic work because its target is a mechanism
The funded trial is basic work, since a controlled trial is a laboratory method however it is paid for
options.misconception: classifies work by the rigour of the method rather than by the question it is set to answer

options.text: The laboratory study is applied work, because anything measured on people can be put to a use
options.misconception: treats any finding as applied merely because a use for it might later be found

questions.explanation: The dividing line runs through the purpose of the question, not through the method or the paymaster. Applied work is set up to inform a decision somebody has to make, which is what the funded training trial is: there is a schedule to adopt or reject, and the trial is designed to bear on that choice. Basic work is set up to describe or account for a process, and the motor-skill study is that even though its sponsor, if any, has no decision riding on the answer. The two are not ranked, and the same study can be both: a mechanism found in a laboratory is frequently what makes a later applied trial worth running. Classifying by rigour confuses the quality of the work with its aim. Treating any measurable finding as applied erases the distinction, because nearly everything eventually gets used. Restricting applied work to medical settings is simply wrong, since most applied work in the field is educational, industrial, forensic or clinical rather than medical.
questions.hint: Ask what the study is being run to decide, not how carefully it is run or who is paying.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Scientist and the Practitioner
questions.learningObjective: state what separates research training from practice training
questions.stem: One training route ends in a doctorate built around original studies and the other in supervised practice with a defined client population. What does the difference between the routes mark?

options.text: A difference in the evidence required, since applied work needs no evidence to justify a decision
options.misconception: exempts applied decisions from the requirement to be justified by evidence

options.text: A difference in standing only, so the two routes trade places in every professional setting
options.misconception: reduces the difference to status and treats the routes as interchangeable

options.text: Different places of work, one producing knowledge and one applying an established body of knowledge
Different kinds of question, since a practitioner is not permitted to raise a researchable question
options.misconception: denies practitioners any role in framing questions that could be studied

questions.explanation: The routes differ in what the person is trained to do with an existing body of knowledge. The research route is built around producing a small addition to that body: designing a study, defending a design, surviving a result that did not come out, and reporting it in a form others can check. The practice route is built around delivering that body to a person with a problem, which requires judgement about a case, a duty to the person in front of you, and a different kind of accountability, since the cost of a mistake falls on one individual rather than on the average of a sample. Neither route makes questions illegitimate, applied work generates questions that the next study should answer, and the best services draw on both. A difference in standing is not what the difference is, and the two routes differ in kind rather than in rank.
questions.hint: Ask what each route prepares a person to do with what is already known.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Two Levels of Explanation of One Event
questions.learningObjective: explain why a molar and a molecular account can both be right
questions.stem: One rider crashes at a junction and another brakes early. The first account is that the rider made a judgement error and the second is that the braking reflex failed. What does the pairing show about the two levels?

options.text: The judgement account is the true one and the reflex account is a detail with no explanatory power
options.misconception: ranks the molar level as the only genuine explanation

options.text: The reflex account reduces the judgement account, so the first is discarded once the second is given
options.misconception: assumes the molecular level replaces rather than complements the molar one

options.text: The two levels compete to answer one question, so at most one of them can be correct
options.misconception: treats two levels as rival answers to a single question

options.text: The two accounts answer different questions about one event, so each can hold while the other is silent

questions.explanation: The two accounts are answering different questions, and identifying the questions is what dissolves the apparent competition. The judgement account asks about the rider's state: what he thought the junction required and why he was in a hurry, which is a question about a person in a situation. The reflex account asks about the mechanism: how the signal from the road reached the leg and how fast it could be acted on, which is a question about a system. An account at one level is not competing with an account at the other, and a complete account of the crash would need both, since a rider in a state of mind he could not have had, driving a body whose reflexes he could not have used, would still be a different event. The other three readings each assume the levels are rivals, which is the error the pairing is designed to expose.
questions.hint: Write down the question each account is trying to answer before deciding which is right.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: A Laboratory Opens in 1879
questions.learningObjective: place the founding of the discipline in time and say what it marked
questions.stem: In 1879 a small university town in Saxony began timing reactions to metronomes and recording the impressions of trained observers. What had happened there?

options.text: The first hospital for the mentally ill had opened, marking the point at which an illness acquired a cause
options.misconception: reads the opening of a laboratory as the founding of an institution for the ill

options.text: The first department of neurology had opened, marking the point at which the nerve cell was described
options.misconception: dates the description of the nerve cell to the opening of the laboratory

options.text: The first school of education had opened, marking the point at which children began to be tested
options.misconception: treats the founding of the discipline as the beginning of educational testing

options.text: The first laboratory dedicated to the new discipline had opened, marking the point at which it claimed a separate identity

questions.explanation: The date and the place together mark the moment the subject stopped being a chapter of philosophy and physiology and became a discipline with its own building, its own appointments and its own method. Timing reactions was not a decorative choice: it converted a philosophical argument about whether mind and body interact into a quantity that two observers could disagree about in a measurable way, which is the condition for a subject to accumulate data rather than positions. The observers were trained rather than casual, because the aim was to report an experience that was supposed to be shared, and that aim is exactly where the method later ran into trouble. The distractors each attach a real historical development to the wrong date or the wrong place: the description of the nerve cell came a few years later and elsewhere, the hospital and the school of education have their own histories, and none of them is the event the date marks.
questions.hint: Ask what a laboratory with its own building and its own method signals about a subject's status.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The School That Catalogued Elements
questions.learningObjective: identify structuralism and the claim it made about the mind
questions.stem: One early school held that a mind is built from a small number of basic elements put together, and that the discipline's task was to name those elements and state the laws by which they combine. Which school is meant?

options.text: Structuralism, which took conscious experience to be assembled out of elementary sensations and ideas
Functionalism, which took the elements to be tools by which a person adapts to a demanding world
options.misconception: names the school that asked what an operation is for rather than what it is made of

options.text: Behaviourism, which took the laws of combination to be training schedules reinforced by outcomes
options.misconception: confuses the combination laws of ideas with reinforcement schedules

options.text: The gestalt school, which took the laws of combination to be unanalysable and to be felt as wholes
options.misconception: attributes a refusal to analyse down to elements to a school that explicitly denied it

questions.explanation: Two commitments define the school: that experience is analysable into a small set of irreducible elements, and that there is a science to be built on the analysis, with laws of combination analogous to the laws governing a chemical compound. The programme is a serious one, and the intuition behind it, that a rich inner life is assembled rather than primitive, has been vindicated in fields it did not anticipate. What it could not deliver was agreement about the elements, because the method it used depended on a report by the observer about their own experience, and trained observers did not converge. Functionalism kept the element analysis out of the centre and asked about purpose instead. Behaviourism removed experience from the vocabulary altogether. The gestalt school rejected the analysis in exactly the terms this option uses, holding that an organised whole is not the sum of its parts, so it cannot be reached by adding them.
questions.hint: Ask which school tried to state a set of laws of combination, and for what the elements combined were supposed to be.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Why Introspection Was Abandoned as a Method
questions.learningObjective: explain the reasons a self-report method failed as the discipline's foundation
questions.stem: A school began by asking trained observers to report the contents of their own awareness, and within a generation that programme was abandoned as a foundation. Explain why it was abandoned.

answer.exemplar: The programme failed for three connected reasons, and it is worth giving them separately because they are usually run together. The first is that trained observers did not agree. Two people watching the same event and reporting what passed through awareness produced markedly different lists, and a method whose output varies with the observer cannot found a science, because there is then no fact about the event to explain. The second is that the training intended to remove the disagreement partly caused it. A discipline that defines the observer's job as holding back a judgement about what is real trains observers to screen out exactly the sort of thing other people report, so the disagreement is not noise to be filtered but a systematic effect of the instructions. The third is that the reports are reports: a person is being asked to describe a process, and the description is produced by the very faculty whose content is in question, so the method cannot be checked against the thing it describes. What follows from this is not that first-person evidence is worthless. It is that a claim resting on it is a claim about what people say, and it needs some independent handle, whether a behavioural measure, a physiological record or a prediction made in advance, before it can carry a weight that exceeds the number of people who said it. The programme was not silly, and its insistence on analysing experience into elements left a permanent mark on the field; what it could not be was a foundation.

questions.explanation: A good answer gives the three reasons separately: observers did not converge, so there was no agreed fact to explain; the training designed to produce agreement produced a screening of experience that made the disagreement systematic rather than random; and a report about one's own processing is generated by the faculty under investigation, so it cannot check itself. It should then draw the correct inference, which is not that first-person evidence is worthless but that it is evidence about reports unless something independent is attached to it.
questions.hint: Ask what would have had to happen for the method to work, and then which of those things did not happen.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The School That Asked What Experience Is For
questions.learningObjective: identify functionalism and the question it made central
questions.stem: A rival school asked not what conscious experience is made of but what it is for, treating the mind as a set of habits that fit an organism to a demanding environment. Which school, and what did it expect a laboratory to produce?

options.text: Neuropsychology, which expected pictures of the cortex taken while a person is performing a task
options.misconception: attaches an imaging method to a school that predates imaging by decades

options.text: Functionalism, which expected measurements of how a mental process helps an organism cope with its surroundings
Structuralism, which expected a catalogue of the basic elements out of which conscious experience is built
options.misconception: names the elemental school and attaches the practical question to it

options.text: Psychoanalysis, which expected case histories showing how an early wish persists into adult life
options.misconception: substitutes the psychodynamic method for the experimental one

questions.explanation: The shift in the question is the whole content of the disagreement. Asking what the elements are invites a chemist's programme, in which the elements are the subject and the laws of combination are the prize. Asking what a process is for invites a programme of measurement of usefulness, in which a mental operation is a solution to a problem the organism faces, and a laboratory would be expected to show how a habit, an image or an idea changes what an organism can do. That question turned out to be the more durable of the two, because it is the question a design of an experiment, an interface or a therapy keeps having to answer. It has a limitation of its own, which is that the purpose of a process is not always visible from the behaviour, and an account that insists everything is there for something has trouble with the cases where nothing is. Structuralism and psychoanalysis did not adopt the practical question, and imaging belongs to a much later period than this argument.
questions.hint: Look for the school whose central question is about usefulness rather than about composition.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The School That Refused to Analyse Down
questions.learningObjective: identify the gestalt school's founding claim
questions.stem: A school founded in the early twentieth century claimed that an organised whole cannot be recovered by listing its parts and adding them, and it built experiments with carefully controlled displays to demonstrate the claim. Which school is described?

options.text: The structuralist school, which argued that whole perceptions are compounds of elementary sensations
options.misconception: attributes a refusal to add up parts to the school that tried hardest to add them up

options.text: The behaviourist school, which argued that whole perceptions are chains of conditioned responses
options.misconception: reads a claim about organisation as a claim about conditioned response chains

options.text: The gestalt school, which argued that organisation is a property of the arrangement rather than a sum of parts
The functionalist school, which argued that whole perceptions exist so an organism can act in a changing world
options.misconception: confuses the purpose argument with the argument about organisational wholeness

questions.explanation: The distinguishing move is the refusal of the additive assumption. The school's argument was that an arrangement has a figure, a grouping and a shape which are not present in any of its parts and do not survive being taken apart, so that a program of analysis into elements loses precisely what it was trying to describe, and no sum of the element reports can put it back. The method matched the claim: displays were built so that the arrangement alone varied while the parts stayed fixed, which is why the experiments are still taught as models of controlled demonstration. The limitation worth naming is that this is an argument about a domain rather than a method for finding out about any domain, and it did not by itself tell investigators how to study the rest of behaviour. The functionalist option substitutes a purpose argument, the structuralist option states the opposite of the school's central claim, and the behaviourist option belongs to a later argument about what counts as a datum.
questions.hint: Ask which school's founding claim was that adding up the parts loses what matters.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: An Influential Account and Its Present Standing
questions.learningObjective: state the evidential standing of the psychodynamic account
questions.stem: An account treating much of mental life as unconscious conflict shaped clinical work for the first third of the twentieth century. Which judgement about its standing now is fair?

options.text: It was discarded at the moment laboratory methods arrived and left behind no working method of any kind
options.misconception: claims the movement left nothing at all, ignoring the method it invented

options.text: It is a purely descriptive scheme, so its statements about causes are confirmed wherever therapy succeeds
options.misconception: declares the causal claims confirmed and simultaneously calls the scheme merely descriptive

options.text: It is historically important, and its central claims about hidden causes are not supported by the evidence now available
It remains the best-supported account, since sustained clinical success settles questions an experiment cannot reach
options.misconception: treats continued clinical use as evidence that would settle the causal claims

questions.explanation: Two things have to be kept apart: what the account contributed and whether its claims are borne out. The contribution is real and permanent. It supplied a method for talking about a person's own account of their difficulties without treating that account as a transcript of what happened, it made it respectable to take a report of inner life seriously as a thing to be understood rather than as a symptom to be corrected, and it produced techniques of free association and interpretation that are still taught. The causal claims fare differently. Assertions about concealed wishes, about a fixed number of early experiences and about a single hidden cause of a symptom cannot be tested in the ways that would support them, and the treatments designed on the basis of those claims have not been shown to work through the mechanisms the account proposes. The clinical-success argument fails because a therapy can help for a reason other than the one it was built on, which is a possibility the account gives no way to exclude. The middle options are self-undermining: one denies any inheritance, and the other calls the claims descriptive while treating them as confirmed causes.
questions.hint: Ask what the account gave the discipline that survives, and then what evidence its causal claims would need.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Programme Announced in 1913
questions.learningObjective: state what behaviourism claimed about the admissibility of inner events
questions.stem: A programme announced in 1913 proposed to make a science of whatever an observer could watch, to use stimulus and response as its working vocabulary, and to set aside consciousness as a term that could not be checked. Which programme is meant, and what did it claim?

options.text: Structuralism, which claimed that only the elemental contents of consciousness could be measured
options.misconception: attributes a testability argument to the school that used introspection

options.text: Functionalism, which claimed that a habit is explained by the pair of stimulus and response that built it
options.misconception: confuses a habit's purpose with the pair of events that conditioned it

options.text: The gestalt programme, which claimed that behaviour has to be described as an organised whole or not at all
options.misconception: reads the stimulus and response restriction as a claim about organised wholes

options.text: Behaviourism, which claimed that only an account in terms of stimulus and response could be put to a test

questions.explanation: The claim was methodological before it was substantive, and the distinction matters. Behaviourism did not assert that a private event is unreal; it asserted that no statement about one could be checked, and that a discipline which builds its data out of unchecked statements has stopped doing science. The methodological consequences were productive and are still in use. A demand for operational definition, an insistence on intersubjectively verifiable observation, and a rule that a construct earns its place by what it lets you predict are all more or less direct descendants of this position, even though the programme that produced them is not in force. What it could not do was stop people from trying, and the rest of the twentieth century is largely the record of that: when internal processes became measurable by reaction time, by the accuracy of an answer and by the latency of a report, the vocabulary that had been declared inadmissible turned out to be the one the data required. The distractors each attach the programme to a school whose central question was different.
questions.hint: Ask which movement made testability, rather than the nature of mind, the decisive question.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What a Restriction to Stimulus and Response Cost
questions.learningObjective: identify two problems created by excluding internal processes from a vocabulary
questions.stem: A research programme restricted its vocabulary to stimulus and response. Which two problems did that restriction create? Select both.

options.text: Nothing could be said about how many items a person holds, since the items themselves are never observable
Internal processes had to be inferred rather than reported, so they were always indirect evidence
Animal studies were ruled out, because a rat's response cannot be counted as behaviour
options.misconception: invents a restriction on species that the programme never imposed

options.text: A private event was described as though it were a stimulus, so a feeling was treated as something outside the person
options.misconception: turns an inference about an inner process into a claim about the environment

A capacity such as the number of items held is not an event in the world and not an overt act; it is a property of a processing system, so under the restriction there is no sentence available that mentions it. The result was not that the capacity was denied but that it went unstudied for a decade while a laboratory measured the wrong things competently, and it was recovered as soon as a way of testing it appeared that did not need the capacity itself to be visible. The second problem is the status of every statement about an internal process, which becomes an inference drawn from something else and has to defend itself accordingly. Neither of these is a refutation of the programme: refusing to treat inference as fact is a discipline worth having, and the discipline kept it. The other two options are not consequences of anything. Animal work was central to the conditioning programme rather than excluded by it, and the confusion in the last option is one the programme was explicitly designed to prevent.

questions.learningObjective: describe what changed in the discipline from the late 1950s
questions.stem: From the late 1950s a movement began treating internal processes again as legitimate objects of study, and models of information processing replaced the stimulus and response pair as the standard way to write about behaviour. What is being described?

options.text: The rise of the cognitive approach, which put internal processing back into the discipline's subject matter
The return of introspection, which made trained self-report the discipline's one true method
options.misconception: confuses a revival of internal processes as data with a revival of self-report

options.text: A tightening of behaviourism, which reached the same conclusion by adding hidden causes to its old vocabulary
options.misconception: treats the change as an internal revision of behaviourism rather than a change of subject

options.text: The founding of cognitive neuroscience, which assigned each processing step to a named area of cortex
options.misconception: credits the movement with an anatomical mapping that came later and separately

questions.explanation: What changed was what counted as a possible object of explanation. Once a response could be decomposed in time, an account in terms of stages became necessary rather than convenient, because the stages were the only things that explained the order in which a response went wrong. The methodological side of the change is worth noticing as much as the content. Internal processes became admissible because they could be inferred from the pattern of errors and the times taken, which is a criterion the earlier programme had set for itself, and the new approach satisfied the criterion the old one had refused to relax. That is why the change is best described as a return rather than a revolution in method. The options each misattribute it: self-report had been discredited, the change of subject was not a revision within the old programme, and mapping processing onto cortex is a later development that was not part of the early argument.

questions.learningObjective: trace the contribution of each tradition to a single contemporary study
questions.stem: A study times a reaction to a stimulus, reports a difference between two conditions, and interprets the difference in terms of internal stages of processing. Synthesise what each element of that study owes to a different tradition.

answer.exemplar: The three elements are separable and each has a different pedigree, which is why the study works as it does. The timed reaction owes most to the experimental tradition: a stimulus and a response, held constant except for the one thing under investigation, with a comparison condition to absorb everything else. Its reason for existing is that a time is a quantity two observers can disagree about, which is exactly the requirement the introspection programme could not meet, and it is why the earliest laboratory work is full of reaction times. The reported difference between conditions owes to the statistical and experimental tradition that grew out of that arrangement, and it carries a qualification the study has to state rather than bury: a difference between conditions is a fact about these conditions, and it does not by itself say why it happened or whether it would appear elsewhere. The interpretation in terms of stages owes to the cognitive approach, and it is the step with the largest inferential gap, because a pattern of times and errors is mapped onto a hypothetical sequence, and several different sequences can produce the same pattern. The synthesis worth drawing is that the three elements are not equally secure. The timing and the comparison are close to observation. The stage model is a hypothesis fitted to the pattern, useful because it makes predictions that can be tested by looking for a signature the alternative would not produce, and exposed because it can be fitted so easily that almost any result has some story attached to it. A reader should ask what observation would have been surprising under the proposed model, since a study that rules nothing out has illustrated rather than tested. The same study also shows what the three traditions are for: the first makes a claim checkable, the second tells the reader how much the claim is worth, and the third proposes what is going on.

questions.explanation: A good answer sorts the three elements by how secure they are: the timed comparison is close to observation, the difference between conditions is a statement about those conditions, and the stage model is a hypothesis fitted to a pattern of times and errors. It should add that several different stage structures can produce one pattern, and that the test of the interpretation is whether it predicts something the alternatives would not.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three elements would still stand if every interpretation of the mechanism were withdrawn.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Steps of a Study in Order
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a study from the review of what is known to the release of data
questions.stem: Put these six steps of a study in the order in which they would ordinarily be carried out.

options.text: State what result would count against the guess, so that the guess is capable of being wrong
Carry out the study with a comparison that leaves the factor under investigation as the only systematic difference
Analyse what was measured, keeping the report of the analysis separate from the guess
Draw the conclusion with its limits stated, and release the data so the work can be repeated
Review what is already known and state the question precisely enough for it to have an answer
Decide how each term in the question will be measured, so that a construct is attached to a number

questions.explanation: The order follows from dependencies, and two of the steps are there precisely because of failures that the discipline has already paid for. The question has to be stated before anything else, because a loose question produces a loose measure, and the choice of measure comes next because a term with no procedure attached cannot enter an analysis at all. Deciding what would count against the guess precedes data collection, not after it, and that is the step most often skipped: a study designed with the analysis already decided in mind is very difficult to falsify, whatever it reports. The comparison is built into the design because anything the design leaves free is free to differ between the conditions and will be read as the cause if the result comes out in the direction the guess predicted. The analysis is reported separately from the guess so a reader can tell the two apart, and the data are released at the end because a conclusion that cannot be checked is a claim rather than a finding, and this is the only step that makes the whole sequence verifiable by anyone else.
questions.hint: Ask which step has to be done before the data exist, and which step makes the rest of the sequence checkable.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: A Term With No Procedure Attached
questions.learningObjective: state what an operational definition contributes
questions.stem: A researcher insists that a term such as attention has no procedure attached to it and cannot therefore appear in a study. What is the researcher demanding?

options.text: That a term be measured once at the start and never revised while a study is under way
options.misconception: forbids refining a measure, which is a normal part of piloting

options.text: That a term be tied to a procedure producing a number before it can be used as evidence
That a term be measurable only by instruments, since a questionnaire is not a procedure
options.misconception: excludes questionnaire measures from the class of procedures

options.text: That a term become usable once several researchers have agreed about its meaning in conversation
options.misconception: treats agreement among colleagues as the test of a construct's admissibility

questions.explanation: The demand is a rule about evidence rather than a rule about vocabulary. A term enters a study by pointing at a procedure: a task the person performs, a number a machine produces, a count someone tallies, a set of questions asked in a fixed way. Once that pointer is in place, two researchers can carry out the study and find out whether they got the same numbers, and a reader can see what the term amounted to in practice. This is also what makes a construct comparable across studies, since two groups using the same procedure and two groups merely agreeing that they are studying the same thing are not in the same position. The restriction was never that instruments are required, and a well-built questionnaire is a procedure with its own problems, chiefly about what a score depends on beyond the thing being asked about. Agreement in conversation is exactly what the rule is meant to replace, and a measure is normally revised after piloting rather than fixed in advance.
questions.hint: Ask what a term has to point at before two people can use it and get the same numbers.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: One Construct Measured Two Ways
questions.learningObjective: explain what follows when one construct is operationalised two ways
questions.stem: One study defines a patient's agitation by the number of seat changes in an hour. Another defines the same term by the score on a self-report inventory. What follows from the two definitions?

options.text: The first definition cannot be checked, because a camera cannot be lied to
options.misconception: rejects an observed count as unverifiable on the ground that it can be faked

options.text: The two studies can disagree about the same patient without either being wrong, since each applied a different rule
The second definition is the true one, since a number from a person outranks a number from a camera
options.misconception: ranks a self-report above an observed count as though proximity were irrelevant

options.text: The two must agree if the underlying trait is stable, since a stable trait has one value to report
options.misconception: assumes one stable trait must produce one identical figure however it is measured

questions.explanation: The disagreement is informative, not a symptom that one of the two studies made an error. The two rules pick out different things: seat changes record movement, and the inventory records what the patient says about being unsettled. Those can come apart in both directions, since a person may be unable to sit still and report no distress, and may sit still and report a great deal, and the size of the disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting. The general point is that an operational definition is a decision about what to count rather than a discovery of what the term means, so a term in a discipline is a family of related procedures rather than a single thing with one true reading. What does not follow is that either is more genuine. A number from a person is a report with its own problems, including the tendency to answer in the way the questions are framed, and a count from a camera is a record of movement and not of distress. Stability over time is a different property from agreement across measures, and a trait can be perfectly stable in both while the two measures still disagree.
questions.hint: Ask what each rule actually counts, and whether a disagreement between them is a contradiction.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: A Guess and an Account
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a hypothesis from a theory
questions.stem: One statement says that presenting two options at once will reduce choice time, and a second says that choice needs a comparison that the brain runs by accumulating evidence. How should the pair be classified?

options.text: Both are hypotheses, since a theory is only a hypothesis that has been confirmed
options.misconception: makes a theory a confirmed hypothesis instead of an organised body of findings

options.text: Both are theories, since a hypothesis has to hold for every case before it counts as either
options.misconception: requires universal quantifiers before a claim can be called a hypothesis

options.text: The first is a hypothesis, which is testable, and the second is a theory, which organises many findings
The first is a theory, since it is the broader of the two statements about choice
options.misconception: reads broad as the test for a theory rather than as the difference in kind

questions.explanation: The distinction is about kind rather than size. A hypothesis is a claim about a limited case, shaped so that a result could count against it, and the first statement qualifies because it names a manipulation, an outcome and a direction. A theory is a larger structure that connects a number of such claims and says what would follow from the connection, and the second statement qualifies because it explains why any decision of that kind should take the form it does, which puts other findings into the same account. Two consequences follow. A theory is not a hypothesis that has been confirmed; it is confirmed or undermined as a whole, in pieces, and a well-supported theory still leaves some of its claims unsupported. And a theory is not simply the broader statement, since breadth is a property of a sentence as well: a long prediction about everything is still a hypothesis, and it is still testable.
questions.hint: Ask which statement is shaped so a result could come out against it, and which one links several findings together.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What a Result Against the Guess Achieves
questions.learningObjective: state what a study that fails to support a hypothesis has established
questions.stem: A study designed to show that two options slow a choice instead finds that choice is as fast with two options as with one. What has the study established?

options.text: That choice is instantaneous, so no comparison is involved in deciding between two options
options.misconception: reads a failed prediction as proof that no processing occurs at all

options.text: That the discipline has shown choices are made without any comparison, and the old view is finished
options.misconception: turns one unconfirmed prediction into a general claim that the field has settled

options.text: That the study was badly designed, since a well-run experiment cannot produce an unexpected result
options.misconception: treats an unexpected result as evidence of a faulty experiment

options.text: That the proposed slow-down does not hold at the size and task tested, while leaving other accounts untouched

questions.explanation: A negative result is informative and its information has a shape that is easy to overstate. What has been shown is that a particular predicted effect did not appear at the size, on the task, in the population and with the equipment used, and a conclusion stated in exactly those terms is not a discovery about choice in general. Three things remain open, and naming them is the substance of the answer: the effect might be real but smaller than the study could detect, it might appear on a different task, and competing accounts of the same data are untouched by a failure to confirm the one that was proposed. This is why a failed prediction is a good outcome for a discipline, since it narrows the space of accounts and often points at the assumption that was wrong. The stronger readings fail because a null result is evidence about one prediction and not about the mechanism behind it, and because a well-run experiment producing an unexpected result is the experiment working, not failing.
questions.hint: Ask what the study could have detected, and which accounts the result leaves standing.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Two Accounts, One Design
questions.learningObjective: identify which design discriminates between two competing accounts
questions.stem: Two accounts of a serial-position advantage are on the table: one says early items are recalled because rehearsal begins before the list ends, and one says they are recalled because they are still partly active at test. Which study would tell them apart?

options.text: Present a list to recall, then delay recall by a task that occupies the same verbal resources, and see whether the early-item advantage survives
Present the same list twice in one session and compare recall of the first presentation with recall of the second
options.misconception: varies practice rather than the resource the two accounts actually differ about

options.text: Replace the words with pictures and check whether the early-item advantage is still found
options.misconception: changes the material instead of the variable the two accounts predict differently on

options.text: Ask participants after recall which end of the list they remember best, and compare the answer with their score
options.misconception: asks for a report of the effect rather than measuring it against a prediction

questions.explanation: Discriminating between two accounts means finding the variable on which they predict different things, and then moving it. The rehearsal account says the early items are encoded first and therefore encoded when the list was short, so the advantage should depend on a resource that is already occupied when encoding happens. The active-at-test account says the early items are simply still available when the test begins, so the advantage should survive whatever happens between list and test as long as the trace is not disturbed. Inserting a verbal task between the list and the test is the manipulation that separates these, because it occupies the resource the first account needs and leaves the availability of the trace in the second account substantially intact. The distractors each change something other than the difference between the accounts: repeating the list varies practice, swapping the material varies what is remembered, and asking afterwards collects a judgement rather than a prediction about the data.
questions.hint: Ask where the two accounts predict different amounts of the effect, then move that.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Repeating a Study and What Repetition Shows
questions.learningObjective: state what a replication establishes and what it cannot
questions.stem: A team repeats an earlier study in a second laboratory with new participants and a slightly larger sample, and finds a smaller effect in the same direction. What does the repetition add?

options.text: Evidence that the effect is not confined to one laboratory, while leaving its size open to sampling variation
A settled result, since an effect repeated in two laboratories can no longer be an artefact
options.misconception: treats a single successful repetition as the end of the question

options.text: Nothing, since repeating a study with a different sample cannot bear on whether the first was a fluke
options.misconception: denies that an independent repetition is evidence at all

options.text: A reason to prefer the larger sample, since sample size and the validity of a finding are the same thing
options.misconception: equates the size of a sample with the trustworthiness of a conclusion

questions.explanation: The value of an independent repetition is that it moves the finding away from the accidents of one sample and one setting. A result that depends on the particular participants, the particular room or the particular measurement on one occasion can survive indefinitely without repeating, and a second laboratory that finds it in the same direction is evidence against that kind of accident. What repetition does not do is fix the size, and the shrinkage the team observed is itself the expected and unremarkable outcome, since the first estimate carries sampling error and a study planned without the original in hand will often lean on the extreme estimate. A finding is not thereby in doubt; it is better located. Nor is repetition sufficient for certainty, since an error in the shared design is reproduced faithfully every time, which is why a repetition that changes one thing deliberately, such as the population or the material, is worth more than one that changes only the sample.
questions.hint: Ask which accidents a repetition in a new sample rules out, and which accidents it copies.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What Peer Review Does and Does Not Do
questions.learningObjective: state the function and the limits of peer review
questions.stem: A study is read by three specialists before publication and revised, and a reader asks what the reading accomplished. Which judgement is fair?

options.text: It guarantees that the reported sample is representative of everyone to whom the claim applies
options.misconception: credits review with settling the question of who the findings generalise to

options.text: It can expose errors and unsupported claims, while the study remains the responsibility of the people who ran it
It certifies the study as correct, so a published paper is beyond question afterwards
options.misconception: treats review as a certificate of correctness rather than a check

options.text: It is largely a courtesy, since the editorial decision is made without the reviews
options.misconception: dismisses review as decorative when it is part of the editorial decision

questions.explanation: Review is best understood as a filter with a limited mandate, and the limits are structural rather than accidental. Reviewers can catch an analysis that does not match the design, a claim the data cannot carry, an overlooked confound and a description of the method that would not let anyone repeat the work, and all four are common enough to justify the practice. What review cannot do is check the analysis itself against the raw data, since reviewers usually see a summary, and it cannot tell whether a sample is representative, which is a question about the population rather than about the paper. Nor does it transfer responsibility: the design, the honesty of the report and the choice to publish remain with the investigators, and a procedure that reviewers approve is a procedure someone believed they understood. The fact that many published findings later fail to repeat has made the limits more concrete rather than the practice useless.
questions.hint: Ask what a reviewer actually holds, and then which questions that leaves open.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Reporting Only the Analyses That Worked
questions.learningObjective: explain how selective reporting distorts the literature
questions.stem: A group runs twenty analyses on one dataset, reports the three that reached a threshold, and stays silent about the rest. What happens to the apparent finding?

options.text: The result is weakened, since three findings out of twenty is a modest success rate
options.misconception: reads a low proportion of successes as evidence for the finding rather than against it

options.text: The result becomes untestable, since a reader cannot know which analyses were run
options.misconception: makes a reporting omission into an impossibility of testing

options.text: The chance that at least one of the twenty reaches the threshold is far above the threshold itself, so silence inflates the result
Nothing happens, since a threshold is a threshold and three of twenty clear it
options.misconception: treats the threshold as if it applied to each analysis and not to the family of them

questions.explanation: The threshold belongs to one analysis, and a study that runs twenty has created twenty chances to cross it, so the relevant question is the chance that at least one of them crosses. With a threshold of 0.05 and twenty independent analyses that chance is about 0.64, so a set of twenty entirely null analyses produces something that looks significant about two times in three, and silence about the other seventeen is what removes the reader's ability to notice. This is why a claim about how often a procedure helps can be true in the literature and false in the world. It is a reporting problem rather than an analysis problem, which is why the fixes are procedural rather than statistical: state in advance which analysis will be run, publish the outcomes that were not significant, and let the data be examined, so that the number of opportunities for a chance result is visible instead of hidden. The third option mistakes a low success rate for evidence in favour, and the second ignores the multiple chances entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when one threshold is applied twenty times, and whether the reader is told how many tries there were.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Variable Set and the Variable Measured
questions.learningObjective: name the manipulated and the measured quantity in a design
questions.stem: A study varies the number of items on a display and records the time taken to choose one. What is the independent variable, and what is the dependent variable?

options.text: The number of items is the recorded outcome and the choice time is what the experimenter sets
options.misconception: reverses which quantity is set and which is recorded

options.text: Both are dependent, since neither quantity can be set before the study begins
options.misconception: assumes a design in which nothing is manipulated

options.text: Both are independent, since each quantity could in principle be varied by the experimenter
options.misconception: treats a possible manipulation as though it were an actual one

options.text: The number of items is set by the experimenter, and the choice time is the outcome that is recorded

questions.explanation: The pair of labels is defined by what the design does to each quantity, not by how interesting it is. The independent variable is the one the experimenter puts in different conditions, in this case the number of items on display, which makes it the factor whose effect the study is built to estimate. The dependent variable is the one recorded to find out what the manipulation did, the choice time, and calling it dependent is a reminder that its value is expected to depend on the manipulation rather than to stand on its own. Two refinements matter in practice. A variable can be manipulated and also measured, in which case the same quantity is sometimes the independent variable and sometimes the dependent one, depending on the question. And a covariate, a quantity measured because it might account for part of the effect, is neither manipulated nor the outcome, which is why a design with three measured quantities cannot be described by the two labels alone.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity the experimenter put into different conditions and which one was written down.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Choosing an Outcome That Can Move
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a chosen outcome is fit to detect an effect
questions.stem: A team wants to know whether a warning sign changes behaviour, and has three candidate outcomes: a self-report of whether the sign was noticed, the time to first glance at the sign, and the number of times a person looks away during a task. Which is the weakest choice, and why?

options.text: The time to first glance, because a faster first glance can be produced by a change in the eyes rather than in attention
options.misconception: objects to an outcome for a reason that would defeat any measure of attention

options.text: The number of glances away, because counting glances requires equipment the laboratory may not have
options.misconception: rejects an outcome on grounds of equipment rather than on what it can detect

options.text: All three are equally weak, since no indirect measure of attention can be trusted at all
options.misconception: dismisses every indirect measure rather than comparing what each one depends on

options.text: The self-report of noticing, because what a person says they noticed is easily influenced by the demand to appear attentive

questions.explanation: The question to ask of an outcome is what else the measure is sensitive to besides the factor under study, and a self-report of noticing is heavily contaminated by that. A person asked whether they noticed a sign has an interest in a particular answer, can guess the purpose of the study, and reports what a well-mannered participant would report, so the measure moves with the demand as well as with attention. The two indirect measures are contaminated differently, which is what makes them useful: a first-glance time can shift because of arousal or lighting without any change in attention, and glance counts can shift because a task is more or less demanding. The weakness of any of them is therefore a matter of degree and of what the design controls for, and the usual response is to use more than one and check whether they move together, which is exactly what a single self-report cannot do. Rejecting an indirect measure because it is indirect discards the whole practice of the discipline.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Degrees of Freedom in a Three-Group Comparison
questions.learningObjective: compute the within-group degrees of freedom for a one-way comparison

stimulus.body: A one-way analysis of variance compares three conditions. Condition 1 has 8 participants, condition 2 has 9 and condition 3 has 10. Every participant contributes exactly one score, and no participant appears in more than one condition.
stimulus.license: written for this question; no third-party material

questions.stem: A one-way analysis of variance compares three conditions, with 8, 9 and 10 participants contributing one score each. How many degrees of freedom does the within-conditions term have?
questions.explanation: The within-conditions term measures the variation of participants about their own group mean, and its degrees of freedom count the independent pieces of information left once the group means have been taken out. The steps are: the groups contribute 8 plus 9 plus 10, which is 27 observations; a mean is estimated for each of the three conditions, which uses 3 of those; and 27 minus 3 leaves 24. Two checks confirm the figure. The total degrees of freedom for 27 observations is 26, and the between-conditions term for three groups has 2, so 26 minus 2 is also 24. A common error is to divide the sample sizes instead of adding them, which gives a smaller and meaningless number, and another is to stop at 27 and forget that the three group means have already been spent. The number is a count of what is free to vary, not a measure of the size of the effect, and a small study therefore has a coarse scale against which the data are read.
questions.hint: Add the group sizes, then subtract one for each group mean already estimated.

questions.learningObjective: state the function of a control condition
questions.stem: A study compares a group given a new reading schedule with a group given the schedule already in use. What is the comparison group for?

options.text: To provide everything the study would have had without the new schedule, so a difference cannot be credited to the schedule alone
To keep the total number of participants high enough for the analysis to reach significance
options.misconception: treats the comparison group as a way of buying statistical significance

options.text: To confirm that the participants in the new group really did find the schedule harder
options.misconception: uses the control group to verify a measurement rather than to compare outcomes

options.text: To let the study estimate how large the effect would be if every school adopted the schedule

Without one, any difference between the start and the end of the new schedule could be produced by anything else that changed at the same time, including maturation, practice, the season, the tester and the passage of the tests themselves. The comparison group is matched on all of these and differs in the one thing under study, so a difference between the two groups is a difference that the schedule could account for. That is why the choice of comparison is delicate. A no-treatment group answers a narrower question than a standard-treatment group, and a waiting-list group answers a different question again, since it also changes what participants expect. The distractors each replace this function with a procedural or a projected one: a comparison group is not a lever for reaching a threshold, it does not verify a measure, and it says nothing about settings nobody studied.

Blinding the person who scores adds a third protection, since notes and transcripts carry information about the condition and a scorer who knows it will read differently, and this is the protection that matters most where outcomes are judged rather than counted. options.text: The informed collector will unconsciously falsify the records to match what was expected
options.misconception: moves from a shift in treatment to deliberate falsification

options.text: No difference matters, since a protocol is followed the same way whoever collects the data
options.misconception: assumes a protocol removes the influence of the person following it

options.text: The informed collector may treat the groups differently, so any difference in outcome may be a difference in how the data were gathered

The effects are usually small and are not the point; the point is that they fall entirely on one side of the comparison, so a modest shift in the collector's conduct becomes a systematic difference between the groups. The defences follow directly: blind the collector, write the coding rules down before collection begins, and have a second person score records that carry no condition label. questions.stem: Participants in a study on the effect of a word on memory are told that the study concerns the meaning of words. What problem does that instruction create, and what addresses it?

options.text: The instruction can cue the effect, and removing it entirely is the only possible remedy
options.misconception: insists that the instruction be dropped when it can be disguised

options.text: The instruction reduces the effect by making the task harder, so the problem is that it is too demanding
options.misconception: recasts a cueing problem as a difficulty problem

options.text: The instruction can cue the effect under study, and disguising the purpose controls it while the debriefing restores trust
The instruction is harmless, since participants cannot influence memory by being told what is studied
options.misconception: assumes a verbal cue cannot change the performance it precedes

questions.explanation: A demand characteristic is a cue about the hypothesis, and a cue changes what a participant does without changing anything about the manipulation. Told that meaning is under study, people attend to meaning, and a study of the effect of word form on memory now has an extra difference between the conditions: the two are more distinguishable in the participants' minds. The remedy has two parts, and both are needed. A cover story disguises the hypothesis while the data are being gathered, so the cue is removed, and a debriefing afterwards tells the participants what the real question was and why the disguise was used, which is what protects their trust in research and their standing as partners in it. What the remedy does not license is leaving people misled indefinitely, since a cover story with no debriefing trades a small validity problem for a real ethical one. questions.learningObjective: explain what a placebo effect shows and why a comparison is needed
questions.stem: In a trial, participants given an inert pill report less pain than participants given no pill at all, and both groups were told they might receive an active pill. What does the comparison show, and what would be needed to say more?

options.text: That the pill contains a weak active ingredient, since only a chemical can relieve pain
options.misconception: reads an inert pill as containing a weak dose of the drug

options.text: That the reports are unreliable, so no treatment effect can be measured by asking people
options.misconception: generalises from an expectancy effect to the uselessness of all reported outcomes

options.text: That the no-treatment group was unfairly treated and should have been given the inert pill as well
options.misconception: raises an ethical objection that is the opposite of the design's requirement

options.text: That being given something inert changed the report, and separating that from the effect of an active pill needs both an inert and a no-treatment group

questions.explanation: The comparison isolates one contribution: the act of being given a pill and being told it might help is itself enough to change what a person reports. That is a finding about the measurement as much as about the treatment, and it has a practical consequence, since an untreated control group will show the same improvement and attributing it to an active drug would be an error. What the comparison cannot show is how much of the change the active drug adds, because the pill group has both the drug and the occasion for expecting relief. Separating the two needs three groups: an active pill, an inert pill matched in appearance and in the expectations it arouses, and no pill at all. The third group is what identifies the contribution of the occasion; without it, the two pill groups show only that the active pill was better than an inert one. The other options misread the finding in each of the three available directions: as a chemical effect, as a failure of self-report, and as a grievance about the control group.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Two Random Procedures That Are Not the Same
questions.learningObjective: distinguish random selection from random assignment
questions.stem: In one study every name on a list is given an equal chance of being drawn for the sample. In another, the names that were drawn are shuffled among the two conditions. Which study can support a causal claim?

options.text: The second, because assignment to conditions was made independently of anything about the people
The first, because drawing the sample by chance is what removes the two conditions from each other
options.misconception: confuses who ends up in the study with who ends up in which condition

options.text: Both, since a chance procedure of either kind is enough to rule out an alternative explanation
options.misconception: treats any use of chance as settling causation

options.text: Neither, since a causal claim requires every aspect of the study to be random
options.misconception: requires randomness in the setting and the measures as well

questions.explanation: The two procedures answer different questions and only one of them bears on causation. Random selection asks who is in the study, and it is what lets a finding be described as a finding about a population rather than about the people who happened to volunteer. Random assignment asks who is in which condition, and it is what lets a difference between conditions be attributed to the manipulation, because the two groups were formed independently of everything else about their members, so any other difference between them is a matter of chance that can be averaged out by making enough groups and repeating. A study can have the first and not the second, which is the ordinary situation in a field study: the participants are broadly representative and the conditions were formed by who agreed to take part, so a difference can be described but not caused. Having neither leaves a description of the sample that happened.
questions.hint: Ask which procedure decided who went into which condition, and which decided who was in the study at all.

questions.learningObjective: explain how attrition can bias a comparison
questions.stem: A study of a training programme runs two conditions of 60 people each. All 30 dropouts come from the condition they found hardest, and nothing at all is lost from the other. What is the likely effect on the comparison?

options.text: The effect is only a problem if the dropouts are counted, and counting them is optional in a report
options.misconception: makes the bias disappear once the number of departures is stated

options.text: The survivors in the hard condition are the ones who coped, so that condition looks better than it was
The survivors in the hard condition are the ones who failed, so that condition looks worse than it was
options.misconception: reverses which group the departures make look better

options.text: There is no effect, because dropping out is one of the costs a programme genuinely has
options.misconception: treats attrition as an outcome rather than as a threat to the comparison

questions.explanation: The bias runs in the direction of the thing that made people leave, and in this design the distortion is extreme, since one condition has lost half of the people assigned to it. If the hardest condition is the one people abandon, the people left in it are those for whom it was tolerable, and their performance is the performance of the tolerant subgroup rather than of everyone who was assigned. The condition therefore acquires much of the benefit of a milder version of itself, and the difference between the conditions is compressed. A second feature compounds it: a condition reduced from 60 to 30 has also been changed in size, and small groups give unstable averages, so a figure computed from 30 survivors is not the same kind of quantity as one computed from 60, and a few of the survivors happening to have had a bad night can move it a long way. The remedies follow from the diagnosis. Every departure is reported, the analysis is repeated on the participants who completed, and the characteristics of those who left are compared between conditions, which is what tells a reader whether the departure was related to the condition at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the remaining members of the harder condition have in common, and what they no longer represent.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: A Proportion Tested Against a Null Value
questions.learningObjective: compute a one-proportion z score from a counted outcome

stimulus.body: Forty participants choose between two options presented on a screen, and 28 choose the option on the left. The study's null value for the left choice is 0.50. What is the z score for the difference between the observed and the null proportion, using the null value in the standard error?
stimulus.license: written for this question; no third-party material

questions.stem: Forty participants choose between two options on a screen and 28 pick the one on the left, against a null value of 0.50 for the left choice. What is the z score for the difference between the observed and the null proportion, using the null value in the standard error?
questions.explanation: The steps are: the observed proportion is 28 divided by 40, which is 0.70; the null proportion is 0.50; the difference is 0.20; and the standard error built from the null proportion is the square root of 0.50 times 0.50 divided by 40, which is 0.0791. Dividing 0.20 by 0.0791 gives 2.53. Three things are worth flagging about the result, and the first two concern the size of the sample. A z score of 2.53 is conventionally read as unlikely enough to reject the null at a threshold of 0.05, and the two-sided probability from the normal curve is 0.011. The exact binomial calculation on the same counts gives 0.017 rather than 0.011, because a normal curve is a poor description of a distribution whose tails are this thin at 40 trials, and where the counts are this small the exact route is the one to report. The second point is that a z score expresses the difference in units of sampling error, so it says how surprising the count was and not how large the effect is; 0.70 against 0.50 is a difference of 0.20, and that is the number a reader needs in order to judge whether it matters.
questions.hint: Divide the difference between the observed and null proportions by the standard error computed from the null proportion.
