questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Three Conclusions and What the Design Supports
questions.learningObjective: judge which conclusions a design can support
questions.stem: A study gave 30 people a memory training routine for six weeks and tested recall of a word list before and after, finding an improvement of 12 words. Four claims are offered about it. Which two are supported? Select both.

options.text: Recall was higher after the training than before it, in the people who were trained
The design cannot show that the training caused the improvement, since there was no group that received nothing
The training raises recall in every person who takes part, since a group mean hides what happened to individuals
options.misconception: promotes a group average to a claim about every individual

options.text: Twelve words is the largest improvement any training routine could produce, since the list held only twenty words
options.misconception: treats a measured improvement as the ceiling of what is possible

questions.explanation: The first is what the study measured, stated with the population it measured it in: a before and after comparison of the same 30 people, with the improvement in recall. The second is what the design cannot deliver. With no group that received nothing, anything that changed over the six weeks in the same people is a candidate alongside the training, including practice on the test itself, the passage of time and what a list of words means to someone who has been asked to remember things recently, and the improvement cannot be credited to the training alone. A wait-list or untreated comparison group, or assignment of the training at random, would be what removes those alternatives, which is why the same routine tested in a controlled design has been reported as producing much smaller gains. The individual claim confuses a mean with a distribution, since some people may gain a great deal and others nothing, and a routine that helps some people and not others is exactly the case a group mean conceals. The ceiling claim inverts the finding: 12 words is the improvement found here, and the list's length tells you how much room there was, not how much could have been taken.
questions.hint: Ask what the design measured, what it could have measured with a different comparison, and what a group mean cannot say about individuals.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What a Person Is Told Before Agreeing
questions.learningObjective: identify the required elements of informed consent
questions.stem: Four requirements for consent to take part are offered. Which two belong to it? Select both.

options.text: A description in plain language of what taking part involves, including how long it will take
A statement that the person may stop at any point without giving a reason and without any penalty
An assurance that taking part cannot be refused once the session has begun
options.misconception: denies the right to withdraw after consent has been given

options.text: An assurance that the person will personally benefit from the study, whatever the outcome
options.misconception: makes individual benefit a requirement rather than something a study cannot promise

questions.explanation: Consent has two halves that are frequently confused. The information half is what the person is told before deciding: what the study is about in ordinary language rather than in the field's own terms, what they will be asked to do, how long it will take, what will be recorded, what is being recorded for a research purpose, who will see it and what the risks and benefits are, including the option of none. The voluntariness half is what makes the agreement stand up: the person is a person of normal understanding, is free of pressure to take part, and can stop at any time, and stopping costs nothing, not a fee, not a mark against them, and not a lecture. A consequence of the second half is that a study has to be designed to survive a withdrawal, which rules out designs that depend on everyone finishing. The two distractors each remove a half: one denies the right to withdraw, and the other attaches a promise of personal benefit that no study about ordinary participants can honestly make, since most of them are asked in order to learn something rather than to be helped.

questions.learningObjective: state the scope of the right to withdraw
questions.stem: A participant tells the researcher halfway through a session that she wants to stop. What does the ethics of consent require next?

options.text: That she is asked to stay until the end of the study, since her data are already collected and would be wasted
options.misconception: weighs the researcher's sunk cost against the person's right to stop

options.text: That she stops, that no reason is demanded, and that the data already collected are treated as she was told they would be
That she gives a reason, so that the researcher can record why the study failed for her
options.misconception: makes an explanation a condition of withdrawal

options.text: That she completes the session, since the consent covered the whole procedure and cannot be taken back
options.misconception: treats consent as a contract for the whole procedure

questions.explanation: The right to withdraw is the part of consent that keeps it honest, and it is unconditional in the ordinary case. A person may stop at any time, may give no reason, and owes the researcher nothing for the time already spent. Two things are commonly confused here. The second is the difference between an ordinary study and a study that is genuinely the person's only access to something, such as a treatment they would otherwise not receive, where continuing to be offered what is available is a separate question about care rather than about consent. Making a reason a condition turns a right into a favour, and the two remaining options treat consent as a promise about the whole session that cannot be broken.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Concealing the Purpose and Explaining It Afterwards
questions.learningObjective: state the conditions under which deception in research is defensible
questions.stem: A study cannot tell participants its true aim without changing how they behave, so it uses a cover story and explains the real aim at the end. Which judgement is right?

options.text: It is defensible as long as the cover story could be believed, since plausibility is the only requirement
options.misconception: reduces the requirement to whether the deception would be believed

options.text: It is defensible as long as the records are anonymous, since anonymising them removes the ethical problem
options.misconception: believes that anonymising the data removes the harm done by deceiving people

options.text: It can be defensible when the risk is minimal, the deception is not itself the point, and a debriefing restores understanding
Any deception is unacceptable, so a study that needs one should be abandoned however small the risk
options.misconception: rules out deception in every case, including the minimal-risk cases the standard allows

Anonymised records protect a person's identity in the data and do nothing whatever about being misled while taking part.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Comparing One Risk with Another
questions.learningObjective: rank research procedures by the risk they carry
questions.stem: Four procedures are proposed for a study. Which one is the minimal-risk kind of procedure?

options.text: Asking a person to undergo a scan that delivers a dose of radiation to the head
options.misconception: treats a radiation exposure as no greater in risk than filling in a questionnaire

options.text: Asking a person to give a blood sample, on the grounds that a small needle is less risky than a question about feelings
options.misconception: ranks procedures by how ordinary they look rather than by the risk they carry

options.text: Asking a person to sit through a mild unpleasant stimulus, on the grounds that the discomfort passes quickly
options.misconception: dismisses a risk on the ground that it is short-lived

options.text: Asking a person to fill in a short questionnaire about their sleep, changing nothing about their life

questions.explanation: Minimal risk is defined by comparison rather than by a list. A procedure is minimal-risk when its risks are no greater than those a person meets in ordinary life or in a routine medical or psychological test, and the questionnaire is minimal-risk precisely because answering questions about one's sleep is something people already do, with no exposure and no change to the person. The other three exceed that line in different ways and for different reasons, which is worth seeing rather than asserting. A radiation dose is a physical exposure whose amount has to be justified against the information it buys, and it is not something a person meets in ordinary life. A needle is not large but it is a physical intervention, and the comparison offered for it inverts the scale, since a question about how a person feels carries its own risk of embarrassment and distress. Discomfort is a risk in its own right whatever its duration, and brief does not mean small.
questions.hint: Ask what risks a person already meets in ordinary life or in a routine check-up.

The data become smaller to store, since a code is shorter than a name
options.misconception: treats coding as a storage technique rather than a separation of identity from data

options.misconception: makes a code a lookup key that is available to the whole research team

options.text: Participants can no longer object, since a code removes the last trace of who they were

Storage size is not what a code is for, and a code is not a lookup available to the team, since making it one would undo the separation entirely. questions.learningObjective: state what prospective ethical review adds
questions.stem: A protocol is examined by a panel that includes nobody who stands to benefit from the answer, and this happens before a single participant is recruited. What does the panel add that a check after the study cannot?

questions.learningObjective: judge which positions on the ethics of research are defensible

questions.stem: A study of a new training routine reports p = 0.03 for the difference between trained and untrained groups. Which reading of that figure is correct?

options.text: The chance that the routine in fact makes no difference, which is the figure that settles the question
options.misconception: reads a p value as the probability that the null statement is true

options.text: The chance that the finding will fail to repeat, so a small value predicts a strong result
options.misconception: reads a p value as a forecast about replication

options.text: The share of the improvement that the routine caused, so a small value means a small effect
options.misconception: reads a p value as the proportion of an effect that is explained

options.text: The chance of a difference this large or larger if the routine in fact makes no difference at all

questions.explanation: A p value is a conditional probability about data, not about hypotheses, and the conditioning is what the wording has to carry. It is the probability of a result at least as far from what the null predicts as the one obtained, given that the null is true. The four misreadings each move that probability to a different object. Putting the probability on the null makes the figure answer a question no calculation can answer, since a p value is computed under an assumption and carries no information about how likely that assumption is. Putting it on replication confuses a statement about the data with a statement about the future, and a study with a small p value still fails to repeat sometimes. Putting it on the effect treats a measure of evidential surprise as a measure of magnitude, which is why a very small p value can sit next to a change too small to matter. The conditional reading also explains why a p value is not a verdict: a small one means the data would be surprising under the null, not that the alternative is established.
questions.hint: Write down what is being held fixed, and what the probability is a probability of.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Statement a Test Is Set Up to Challenge
questions.learningObjective: state the role of the null hypothesis in a test
questions.stem: Before collecting any data, a group writes down that two conditions will not differ in the number of errors made. What is the status of that statement?

options.text: It is the research hypothesis, since it is the statement the study is designed to support
options.misconception: reads a pre-stated expectation as the claim the study is trying to confirm

options.text: It is a definition, since it fixes in advance what the two conditions are
options.misconception: treats a prediction about no difference as a description of the conditions

options.text: It is a conclusion, since it is the answer the study has already settled on
options.misconception: treats a pre-stated expectation as the result the study will obtain

options.text: It is the null hypothesis, which fixes what a result would count against, and it is examined rather than assumed

questions.explanation: The null hypothesis earns its place by making a test possible, and its role is to supply the distribution against which a result is judged. Until something like it is fixed, there is no way to say how surprising a set of numbers is, because surprise is always surprise relative to what was expected. It also fixes the exact question a test asks, which is not whether the two conditions differ but whether the data are far enough from what no difference predicts to be worth acting on, and that is why the wording matters: a null about no difference is not the same claim as a null about a particular direction or a particular size. The statement is examined rather than assumed, and a small p value is a reason to set it aside in favour of a competing account, not a demonstration of what is true. Reading it as the claim being confirmed puts the study in the position of looking for agreement, which is the arrangement that produces the confirmation problems the discipline has worked to avoid.
questions.hint: Ask what a result is compared against in order to be called surprising.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Two Kinds of Wrong Answer
questions.learningObjective: apply the definitions of the two kinds of error to a design
questions.stem: A study uses a threshold of 0.05, and its design is such that 80 percent of real effects of the size the team is looking for will be detected. Which pair of figures and names is right?

options.text: About 5 in 100 studies with no real effect will report one, which is a Type I error, and 20 in 100 real effects will be missed, which is a Type II error
About 5 in 100 studies with no real effect will report one, which is a Type II error, and 20 in 100 real effects will be missed, which is a Type I error
options.misconception: swaps the two error names while keeping the rates attached to the right outcomes

options.text: About 5 in 100 real effects will be missed, which is a Type I error, and 20 in 100 null studies will report one, which is a Type II error
options.misconception: attaches each rate to the wrong outcome as well as the wrong name

options.text: About 25 in 100 studies with no real effect will report one, since either side of the threshold counts as a detection
options.misconception: treats a two-sided threshold as two independent chances of a false report

questions.explanation: The two rates have different denominators, and keeping them apart is most of the work in reading an error analysis. The first rate is over studies in which there is no effect, and the threshold of 0.05 is by construction the share of those that will reach it, so about 5 in 100 of them will be reported as finding something, and concluding that something is there when it is not is a Type I error. The second rate comes from the 80 percent of real effects the design detects: the remaining 20 percent of 100 real effects are missed, and failing to detect an effect that is there is a Type II error. The names are usually remembered by the first letter of the false conclusion, since Type I is the effect that is not there and Type II is the effect that is, and the denominators follow the same split. The last option treats a two-sided threshold as two independent chances, which inflates the rate without any basis in the design.
questions.hint: Keep the denominators straight: one rate is over studies with nothing there, the other is over effects that are there.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: How Large Is the Difference, Not Just Surprise
questions.learningObjective: convert a difference in group means into a standardised effect size
questions.stem: Two groups of 20 score a mean of 14 and 11 respectively, and the standard deviation in each group is 4. Which set of figures is right?

options.text: An effect size of 0.75, and a p of 0.02, so the routine accounts for about 2 percent of the variation in scores
options.misconception: reads a p value as the share of variation an intervention explains

options.text: An effect size of 0.75, which becomes a t of 2.37 on 38 degrees of freedom with a two-sided p of 0.023
An effect size of 0.75, which becomes a t of 2.37, with a two-sided p of 0.018 taken from the normal curve
options.misconception: reads the p off the normal curve as though a t on 38 degrees of freedom were a normal deviation

options.text: An effect size of 0.21, since the difference of 3 is divided by the sum of the two means rather than by a spread
options.misconception: divides a mean difference by a sum of means instead of by a pooled spread

questions.explanation: The effect size divides the difference between the means by the spread within the groups, and here that is 3 over 4, which is 0.75. The conversion runs in the other direction and is where most of the arithmetic is: with 20 people in each group the t is the effect size multiplied by the square root of 20 times 20 over 40, which gives 2.37, and the degrees of freedom are 40 people minus 1, which is 39 in total, of which 38 are left once the two group means are taken out. A t of 2.37 on 38 degrees of freedom gives a two-sided p of 0.023, and the normal curve gives 0.018, which is close enough to mislead and different enough to matter at the third digit, since the t distribution is more spread out. The standard error of the difference is worth stating as well: 4 times the square root of 1 over 20 plus 1 over 20, which is 1.265, and 3 divided by 1.265 is the same 2.37. A share of variation explained is a different quantity, obtained by squaring a correlation or an effect size and is not a p value.
questions.hint: Divide by the pooled spread, then multiply by the square root of the harmonic grouping term, and count what is left over.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: A Small Table and Three Ways to Test It
questions.learningObjective: compare the asymptotic and exact tests of a fourfold table
questions.stem: A trial records 18 improved and 12 unimproved on the new treatment, against 10 improved and 20 unimproved on the old. Which reading is right?

options.text: The uncorrected statistic is 8.57 on 1 degree of freedom, since each row contributes the same 16 squared
options.misconception: adds the two rows' contributions instead of all four cells' deviations

options.text: The uncorrected statistic is 4.29, and since it exceeds 3.84 the finding is established whatever the exact test says
options.misconception: lets the asymptotic p override the exact test on these cell counts

options.text: The uncorrected statistic is 4.29 on 1 degree of freedom, and the exact two-sided test gives about 0.069, so the result sits closer to the threshold than it looks
The uncorrected statistic is 4.29 on 1 degree of freedom, and the exact test agrees with it, so the finding is secure
options.misconception: assumes an exact test reproduces the approximation when the cell counts are this small

questions.explanation: With 60 observations and cells in single figures, the two routes give noticeably different answers and the difference is the finding. The uncorrected statistic sums, over all four cells, the squared gap between the observed and the expected count divided by the expected count: the expected counts are 14, 16, 14 and 16, the gaps are 4 in every cell, and the four contributions are 1.14, 1, 1.14 and 1, which sum to 4.29 on one degree of freedom, giving 0.038. The exact conditional test asks how often a table this extreme arises given the margins alone, and the answer is about 0.069, with the one-sided version about 0.035. The corrected statistic, which subtracts half a count from each gap before squaring, gives 3.28 and about 0.070, so the correction and the exact test agree closely. The rule that follows is not that the larger number is the true one but that with cells this small the exact calculation should be reported, and that a conclusion resting on 0.038 rather than 0.069 is resting on an approximation that the data cannot support.
questions.hint: Work out the four expected counts, sum the four contributions, and then ask what the margins alone would produce.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Two Ways of Expressing One Treatment Effect
questions.learningObjective: compute a relative risk, an absolute reduction and a number needed to treat
questions.stem: In a trial, 30 of 100 people given a treatment have the outcome of interest and 12 of 100 given the comparison treatment do. Which set of figures is right?

options.text: A relative risk of 0.4, since dividing the comparison rate by the treated rate gives the more useful figure
options.misconception: inverts the ratio so that a harmful treatment reads as a protective one

options.text: A relative risk of 2.5 and a number needed to treat of 2.5, since the ratio is the count of people who must be treated
options.misconception: uses the relative risk itself as the number needed to treat

options.text: A relative risk of 2.5, an absolute reduction of 18 percentage points, and about 6 people treated for one to be spared
A relative risk of 2.5 and an absolute reduction of 18 points, which together make the two treatments equivalent in effect
options.misconception: treats a doubled rate and an 18-point shift as the same practical matter

questions.explanation: The three figures are the same result measured against three different baselines, and which one to use depends on the decision. The treated rate is 0.30 and the comparison rate is 0.12, so the relative risk is 0.30 over 0.12, which is 2.5, and the absolute reduction is 0.30 minus 0.12, which is 0.18, or 18 percentage points. The number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute reduction, 1 over 0.18, which is 5.6 and so means 6 people treated for one to be spared. A relative risk keeps the baseline in view and is the right form when the untreated rate varies between populations, which is why it dominates the reporting of observational work; an absolute figure is the right form when the question is how many people a decision would spare here, since the same 2.5 against a baseline of 1 percent spares almost nobody and against a baseline of 40 percent spares a great many. The inversion in the third option makes a harmful treatment look protective, and the fourth confuses a ratio of rates with a count of people.
questions.hint: Divide the treated rate by the comparison rate for one figure, subtract for another, and take the reciprocal of the subtraction for the third.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Conventional Threshold
questions.learningObjective: explain what the 0.05 threshold is and is not
questions.stem: One group calls a result with p = 0.06 a trend and another calls a result with p = 0.04 significant. Which judgement is fair?

options.text: A p of 0.06 is nearly significant, so calling it a trend describes a result that is close to the criterion
options.misconception: treats the distance from an arbitrary threshold as a degree of evidence

options.text: The threshold binds confirmatory analyses only, so exploratory work has no criterion to meet at all
options.misconception: grants exploratory analyses a complete exemption from any standard

options.text: The first group should have reported the figure to more places, since the second decimal is where the evidence lies
options.misconception: treats the second decimal place as carrying the evidential weight

options.text: The threshold is a convention rather than a law, so the two results are not different in kind and the first phrasing is courtesy

questions.explanation: The threshold is a decision about what rate of false positives a reader is prepared to accept, and it was set by convention rather than derived, which is why 0.05 and 0.01 and 0.10 are all in use and none of them is correct in a deeper sense. Two results falling on either side of it are therefore not different in kind, and the useful response to a study is not to ask which side it landed on but how large the effect is, how precisely it was measured, and whether it was predicted beforehand. Calling 0.06 a trend is ordinary and harmless as a description, provided it is not used to smuggle in a conclusion, and the same applies to the reverse habit of describing 0.04 as a finding when the effect is of no practical size. Reporting the exact figure is good practice, and the two-sided version of a p value is already a rounded convention, but precision in the second decimal is not a substitute for a measure of the effect. Exploratory work still has to be described honestly, whatever its status.
questions.hint: Ask where the number 0.05 came from, and what a reader should want instead of a side of a line.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Surprise Is Not Size
questions.learningObjective: distinguish statistical from practical significance
questions.stem: A study of 400 people finds a difference in a reaction time of 4 milliseconds, and a study of 12 people finds a difference of 200 milliseconds that is not conventionally significant. What follows?

options.text: The first result is detectable and the second is not, while the second difference is far larger, so the two do not rank the effects
The second is the more important finding, since a large difference is more useful to have detected than a small one
options.misconception: ranks an undetected large effect above a detected small one on practical grounds

options.text: The first is negligible, since four milliseconds is below the smallest change anyone could notice
options.misconception: invents a minimum perceptible change and declares the measured effect worthless

options.text: Both are equal in size, since a p value is a measure of how large an effect is
options.misconception: reads a p value as a direct measure of effect magnitude

questions.explanation: The two results answer different questions and neither settles the other's. A p value says how far a result sits from what no difference would predict, measured in units of the study's own sampling error, so a large enough sample can make a very small difference detectable and a small sample can leave a large one undetermined. That is the whole of the first result: with 400 people, 4 milliseconds clears a threshold, and whether that matters is a separate question about what people and tasks can notice. The second result is not a smaller finding, it is an undecided one, and the right response is to ask what a study of that size could have detected, which is a question about the design rather than about the effect. Treating the two as comparable runs a p value in place of a magnitude, and the minimum perceptible difference in the third option is a real quantity for some judgements and not for others, so it cannot be assumed to exist for every task. The last option is the misconception the item is about.
questions.hint: Ask what each study could have detected, and what question the p value was answering.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What the Degrees of Freedom Count
questions.learningObjective: state what a degrees-of-freedom figure represents
questions.stem: A comparison of three groups of 8, 9 and 10 people reports 24 degrees of freedom for the within-conditions term. What does that number represent?

options.text: The number of measurements made on each person, since each person contributes one degree of freedom
options.misconception: assigns a degree of freedom to each person's single score

options.text: The independent pieces of information left for the variation of people about their own group means, once three means are estimated
The number of people in the smallest group, so the analysis is limited by the weakest group
options.misconception: reads degrees of freedom as the size of the smallest comparison group

options.text: The number of possible group means, which is three fewer than the number of people
options.misconception: counts the group means rather than the information left after them

questions.explanation: Degrees of freedom count the independent pieces of information that remain once the parameters already estimated have been paid for, and the phrasing matters because it is what stops a figure being read as a sample size. Here 27 scores have been collected, 3 group means have been computed from them, and 3 pieces of information have been spent on those means, leaving 24 that can vary independently about the group means. The same arithmetic read from the other end gives the same answer: 27 people supply 26 independent comparisons in total, the 3 conditions use 2 of them, and 26 minus 2 is 24. What the number is not is any of the alternatives. It is not the smallest group, because nothing in the analysis is limited to the smallest cell, and a design with unequal groups is still a valid design. It is not a count of measurements per person, and it is not the number of means. The number also says something about resolution: with few degrees of freedom the scale is coarse, so a study of 24 gives a poorer read on a small effect than a study of 240 does.
questions.hint: Count the measurements, then subtract one for each quantity already estimated from them.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Choosing a Test to Match the Design
questions.learningObjective: match a data structure to the appropriate test
questions.stem: Four analyses are described. Which set of tests is the right match for all four?

options.text: Two independent groups of 30 by a comparison of means, the same 30 measured twice by a goodness-of-fit test, six categories by an analysis of variance, and three groups of 10 by a paired comparison
options.misconception: misaligns the repeated-measures and the frequency designs while keeping the others

options.text: Two independent groups of 30 by a comparison of means, the same 30 measured twice by a paired comparison, six categories by a goodness-of-fit test, and three groups of 10 by a one-way analysis of variance
Two independent groups of 30 by a paired comparison, the same 30 measured twice by a comparison of means, six categories by a goodness-of-fit test, and three groups of 10 by a paired comparison
options.misconception: swaps the paired and independent tests in the first two cases

options.text: Two independent groups of 30 by a goodness-of-fit test, the same 30 measured twice by a paired comparison, six categories by an analysis of variance, and three groups of 10 by a comparison of means
options.misconception: matches a test to each design on the number of groups rather than on the data structure

questions.explanation: A test is chosen by the shape of the data and the comparison being made, not by the number of groups. Two independent groups of 30 supply two sets of scores with no pairing, so a comparison of means is the match, and it uses the between-people variation for its standard error. The same 30 people measured twice supply paired scores, so a paired comparison is the match, and it is more sensitive precisely because the between-people variation cancels. Six categories in which only the counts matter ask whether the observed frequencies match some expected pattern, which is what a goodness-of-fit test is for, and it is the test that goes with nominal categories rather than with measured scores. Three groups of 10 ask whether three means differ, and the one-way analysis of variance is the test built for that, with two degrees of freedom between the groups. Each of the distractors gets at least one of these wrong, and the errors are instructive: pairing a test to a design by group count rather than by data structure is the commonest of them.
questions.hint: Ask for each case whether the scores come from separate people or the same people, and whether the data are numbers or counts.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: How Wide an Interval Around a Share
questions.learningObjective: compute a margin of error for a proportion

stimulus.body: A survey of 200 people finds that 15 report a particular habit. Using the observed share, what is the margin either side of that share for a 95 percent interval?
stimulus.license: written for this question; no third-party material

questions.stem: A survey of 200 people finds that 15 report a particular habit. Using the observed share of 0.075, what is the margin either side of it for a 95 percent interval?
questions.explanation: The share is 15 over 200, which is 0.075, and the standard error of a share is the square root of the share times one minus the share divided by the number of observations, which is the square root of 0.075 times 0.925 over 200, and that comes to 0.0186. The margin is 1.96 times that standard error, which is 0.0365, so the interval runs from 0.038 to 0.112. Two things belong with the figure. The width is driven by the sample size and not by the size of the share, so a survey of 2,000 would give a margin of about 0.0115, one fifth as wide, and a survey of 200 can never support a claim about a habit held by 7 or 8 percent of people to better than about 4 percentage points either way. And the same formula evaluated at a share of one half gives a margin of 0.069, which is the figure a reader should assume when a survey reports its result without one, since the error is largest when the share is near a half. That is why an interval that is 4 to 11 percent is honest about this finding and an interval reported as 7 percent is not.
questions.hint: Divide the share by its complement, divide by the number of people, take the square root, and multiply by 1.96.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Two Error Rates With Different Denominators
questions.learningObjective: compute false-negative and false-positive counts from a design's rates

stimulus.body: A test is applied to 200 people who have the condition and 800 who do not. The test finds 80 percent of those who have it, and it flags 5 percent of those who do not. First work out how many cases are missed, then how many people without the condition are wrongly flagged.
stimulus.license: written for this question; no third-party material

questions.stem: A test is applied to 200 people who have the condition and to 800 who do not. It detects 80 percent of the cases, and it flags 5 percent of the people who do not have it. First work out how many cases are missed, then how many people without the condition are wrongly flagged.

options.text: 40 cases missed and 4 people wrongly flagged, since 5 percent of 800 is 4 and not 40
options.misconception: misplaces the decimal when applying the rate to the larger group

options.text: 40 cases missed and 50 people wrongly flagged, since 5 percent is most easily applied to the whole thousand
options.misconception: applies the false-flag rate to the combined group instead of to the unaffected group

options.text: 40 cases missed and 40 people wrongly flagged, since 20 percent of 200 and 5 percent of 800 are different counts
20 cases missed and 40 people wrongly flagged, since half of the 40 undetected cases have to be recovered
options.misconception: halves the missed count by treating a rate as if it were a count of a half group

questions.explanation: Each rate has its own denominator and the two rates are about different populations, so they cannot be applied to the same base. The detection rate applies to the 200 who have the condition, and its complement of 20 percent applied to 200 is the 40 cases that go undetected. The false-flag rate applies to the 800 who do not, and 5 percent of 800 is 40 people wrongly flagged. Two figures are worth adding, because they are where the interest usually lies. Total flags come to 160 real plus 40 false, so 200 flags in all, of which 160, or 80 percent, are real, and that high figure is a consequence of the base rate rather than of the test's accuracy. The fourth option is the trap: 5 percent of 1,000 gives 50, which is wrong because the 200 who have the condition were not subject to a 5 percent false-flag rate at all. The two routes to the same conclusion are worth stating explicitly, since a reader who cannot say which denominator a rate belongs to cannot check any of these numbers.
questions.hint: Apply the detection rate to the 200 who have the condition and the flag rate to the 800 who do not, and keep the bases apart.
